title: The Value of Variance: Mitigating Debate Collapse in Multi-Agent Systems via Uncertainty-Driven Policy Optimization
one_liner: This paper measures uncertainty inside multi-agent debate and then trains the system to avoid self-contradiction, peer conflict, and low-confidence answers.
lead: Multi-agent debate can fail in a very specific way: several agents talk for many turns, but the final decision still rests on bad reasoning. This paper treats that failure as a measurable uncertainty problem, then uses that measurement to train a safer debate policy.

problem.h2: Debate can collapse even when many agents participate
paras: In multi-agent debate, several agents propose answers, challenge each other, and then produce a final decision. More discussion does not guarantee a better result because the group can settle on a wrong line of reasoning and then reinforce it across turns. A debate can collapse when that reinforcement keeps errors alive until the final answer.

The hard part is diagnosis. A poor final answer can come from a single agent contradicting itself, from several agents fighting without resolving the core issue, or from the whole system ending with a weak answer. If these failure modes are not measured separately, the training signal stays too blunt.

callout.html: Measure uncertainty at several levels, then train against the specific forms of uncertainty that precede debate collapse.

panels.title: 1. Agents start debating
panels.viz_args: Several agents answer the same question and exchange critiques.
panels.caption: The system begins with multiple candidate answers and several rounds of discussion.

panels.title: 2. One agent contradicts itself
panels.viz_args: Turn 1 says A. Turn 3 says not A.
panels.caption: An agent can be unstable across its own turns.

panels.title: 3. Peers keep clashing
panels.caption: Several agents can keep disagreeing without moving toward resolution.

panels.title: 4. Add uncertainty penalties
panels.viz_args: Reduce reward when self-contradiction, peer conflict, or weak final confidence appears.
panels.caption: Training starts to punish the patterns that usually appear before collapse.

panels.title: 5. Final decision is steadier
panels.viz_args: The group reaches a cleaner answer after fewer unstable turns.
panels.caption: The debate becomes more reliable because unstable behavior is explicitly discouraged.

steps.text: Let several agents answer, critique, and revise across multiple turns.
Track uncertainty inside each agent, across agents, and in the system's final output.
Give lower reward when an agent contradicts itself, when the group keeps conflicting, or when the final answer stays weak.
Train the agents with those penalties so the debate process shifts away from collapse patterns.
Check whether the trained system answers more questions correctly and with less disagreement.

paras: The paper changes the reward used during debate training. Instead of rewarding only the final answer, it also scores the stability of each agent, the agreement pattern among agents, and the quality of the final decision.

hidden.name: how much instability appears inside agents, between agents, and in the final answer
paras: Hierarchical uncertainty is a structured measurement of instability. At the first level, it asks whether one agent changes its position across turns. At the second level, it asks whether different agents keep conflicting with each other. At the third level, it asks whether the final system output still looks weak or undecided.

This hidden quantity matters because collapse is not one event. It is a chain of unstable steps. Measuring the chain lets training target the actual source of failure instead of only observing the bad final answer.

heat.caption: The darkest cells mark the patterns most associated with collapse: self-contradiction and unresolved peer conflict.

reads.html: A debate can look active while still being unstable. The useful signal is not just the final answer. It is where the instability starts.
The method uses separate uncertainty measurements for the agent level, the interaction level, and the final output level, which means training can penalize the exact failure mode that appears.

paras: The training rule helps because it turns early warning signs into direct learning pressure. If an agent contradicts itself, that instability now lowers reward. If the group keeps fighting without resolving the issue, that conflict also lowers reward. Over many debate episodes, the policy shifts toward paths that avoid those penalties.

This improves final accuracy because the group is not rewarded for noisy debate that happens to end with an answer. It is rewarded for a process that stays internally consistent and reaches a clearer outcome by reducing unstable turns before they spread through the group.

stages.s: Track weakness in the final answer
Lower reward when these signals rise
A steadier debate policy with fewer collapse episodes

math.words: Start with the reward for getting the task right, then subtract penalties for three kinds of uncertainty: inside one agent, across agents, and in the final answer.
math.equation: total_reward = task_reward - a * self_uncertainty - b * peer_uncertainty - c * output_uncertainty
symbols: reward for answering the task correctly
how much one agent contradicts itself across turns
how much different agents keep conflicting
how weak or undecided the final answer looks
weights that control how strongly each penalty matters

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a debate episode answers the task correctly, so task_reward is 10.
Suppose self_uncertainty is 2, peer_uncertainty is 3, and output_uncertainty is 1.
Set a, b, and c to 1 for a simple example.
Then total_reward is 10 minus 2 minus 3 minus 1, which is 4.
A cleaner debate with the same final answer but lower uncertainty would earn more reward, so training prefers the cleaner path.

math.note: The page uses a simple additive form to show the training logic: right answers count, but unstable debate steps lower the score.

charts.title: Debate without uncertainty penalties
charts.note: The system still debates, but unresolved conflict stays high because training does not punish the unstable path.

charts.title: Debate with uncertainty-driven optimization
charts.note: The final answer improves because the policy learns to avoid instability before it reaches the last turn.

items.html: If the system measures instability badly, it can punish useful disagreement and train the agents toward shallow consensus.
If the uncertainty penalties dominate the task reward, agents may stop exploring alternative answers and settle too early.
Some hard questions require several candidate answers before the group can test them. Punishing every conflict would remove that useful search behavior.
The method works when uncertainty is measured carefully and penalties are tuned so that useful exploration remains possible while repeated instability becomes costly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small debate environment with three to five agents answering math word problems, tool-use tasks, or short reasoning questions. Log each turn, then compute three signals: self-contradiction inside each agent, conflict across agents, and weakness in the final answer. Train one system with only task reward and one with the uncertainty penalties. Compare final accuracy, contradiction rate, and unresolved disagreement rate.

The demo proves the paper's claim if the uncertainty-aware system answers more questions correctly while showing fewer unstable debate patterns, because the added penalties teach the group to avoid collapse before the final turn.
demo.closing: A good demo should also show at least one collapse case where the baseline drifts through conflicting turns and the uncertainty-aware policy exits with a cleaner path.
